questions.solution:
To convert the direct speech sentence "He always says to me, 'I am perturbed'" to indirect speech:

The reporting verb "says" is present tense, so the tense of the reported clause ("I am perturbed") remains present ("is").

The phrase "to me" indicates the verb should be "tells" (as "say to someone" becomes "tell someone" in indirect speech).

The pronoun "I" changes to "he" to match the subject.

The conjunction "that" is added, and quotation marks are removed.

The direct speech "I am perturbed" becomes "he is perturbed," making the sentence: "He always tells me that he is perturbed."

Checking the options:

Option 1: "He always tells me that he is mostly perturbed" adds "mostly," which is not in the original.

Option 2: "He always tells me that he is perturbed by change" adds "by change," which is not implied.

Option 3: "He always tells me that he is perturbed" accurately reflects the original sentence.

Option 4: "He always tells me that he is going to be perturbed" shifts to future tense, which is incorrect.

Thus, option 3 is the correct choice.

In the case of Interrogative sentences like this, "said" in Direct Speech is changed into "enquired (of)", "wanted to know", "asked", etc.

In Indirect speech, the verb is always placed after the subject, unlike in Direct Speech.

If there is a question in the Direct Speech whose answer can come as "Yes" or "No" in the Indirect Speech, we should use the conjunctions "if" or "whether".

For example:

Ravi said to me, "Is she studying?" (Direct Speech)

Ravi asked me if she was studying. (Indirect Speech)

Also, when converting direct speech into indirect speech, the present modal verbs (can/may/must/will/shall) should be changed into past modal verbs (could/might/had to/would/should).

Example: She said, "I can speak ten languages." (Direct Speech)

She said that she could speak ten languages. (Indirect Speech)

The following things in the sentence should change when changed from Direct speech to Indirect Speech:

'Said to me' is changed to 'asked me'.

'If' is introduced in the sentence.

'Can you' will be changed to 'I could'

'Help me' will be changed to 'Help him'.

Therefore, the correct answer is option (a): The blind man asked me if I could help him cross the road.

In Direct speech, the verb is always placed before the subject, unlike in Indirect Speech. If there is a question whose answer can come as "Yes" or "No", we remove the inverted commas and add the conjunction "If" or "Whether" in the Indirect Speech and the verb/s "Is/are/am/was/were" before the subject, in Direct Speech.

For example:

Ravi asked me if she was studying. (Indirect Speech)

Ravi said to me, "Is she studying?" (Direct Speech)

The sentence in the Indirect Speech is in Past Perfect Tense.

There are three cases when the Indirect Speech is in Past Perfect Tense.

I. Tense remains the same.

II. Past perfect changes to Present Perfect

III. Past perfect changes to Simple Past

Case 1: Past Perfect (Subject + had + V3 + Object) tense will be kept intact.

For example:

He said that he had just finished the movie. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "I had just finished the movie" (Direct Speech)

Case 2: Past Perfect (Subject + had + V3 +Object) will be converted into Present Perfect (Subject + has/have + V3+Object).

For example:

He said that he had got a new job. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "I have got a new job." (Direct Speech)

Case 3: Past Perfect (Subject + had+ V3 + Object) will be converted into Past Simple (Subject + V2 + Object).

For example:

He said that Arya had sent him a book. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "Arya sent me a book" (Direct Speech). Here, case 3 will be used, as per the options.

The following things in the sentence will change when changed from Indirect Speech to Direct Speech:

Reporting verb 'enquired' changed to 'asked me'.

The verb phrase 'I had gone' changed to 'Did you go'.

Therefore, the correct answer is: (c).

questions.solution:
Imperative Sentences are used to demonstrate Request, Order, Command, etc.

Imperative Sentences begin with Principal verbs like Go, Make, etc.

The reporting verbs like "said", "say", etc. in direct speech are changed into "begged", "beg", etc.

"To" is used before the Principal Verbs in Indirect Speech.

For example:

John said to his assistant, "Bring me a glass of water." (Direct Speech)

John ordered his assistant to bring him a glass of water. (Indirect Speech)

The following things in the sentence should change when changed from Direct speech to Indirect Speech:

'Said to' into 'requested'.

'Please do not' into 'not to'.

Therefore, the correct answer is: The gardener requested the children not to pluck any flowers.

Hence, option (d) is correct.

questions.solution:
In the case of Interrogative sentences like this, "enquired (of)", "wanted to know", "asked", etc. in Indirect Speech is changed into "said" in Direct Speech.

In Direct speech, the verb is always placed before the subject, unlike in Indirect Speech.

For example:

The teacher asked him what his name was. (Indirect Speech)

The teacher said to him, "What is your name?" (Direct Speech)

The tense of the Indirect Speech is in the Past Perfect tense. There are three cases when the Indirect Speech is in Past Perfect Tense.

· Tense remains same

· Past perfect changes to Present Perfect

· Past perfect changes to Simple Past

In these cases, we go by the options.

As per the given options, the given indirect from in past perfect tense is to be changed to the past simple tense.

The following things in the sentence will change when changed from Indirect Speech to Direct Speech:

The reporting verb may remain the same or be changed to 'said'.

'How I had' is changed to 'how did you'

The pronoun 'his' is changed to 'my'.

'Did' is always followed by the base verb. So, option (b) is incorrect.

Therefore, the correct answer is option (c): "How did you persuade my sister?" Shyam asked me.

questions.question: Select the option that expresses the given sentence in reported speech. He said to the mechanic, "Will you have the car ready by tomorrow morning?"

He said to the mechanic, "Will you have the car ready by tomorrow morning?"

options.text: He told the mechanic if he will have the car ready for the next morning.

options.text: He said the mechanic whether he would has the car ready by the following morning.
options.html: He said the mechanic whether he would has the car ready by the following morning.

questions.solution:
The original sentence is a question in direct speech. In reported speech, a question beginning with "Will" changes to "if/whether" and the verb shifts to the conditional "would." The phrase "tomorrow morning" becomes "the next morning" to reflect the time shift in reported speech. Option (a) correctly applies these rules: "asked" indicates a question, "if" introduces the reported question, and "would have" is the correct verb form. The other options contain grammatical errors or incorrect time references.

Option b: He told the mechanic if he will have the car ready for the next morning. "Told" is incorrect for a question (questions use "asked"). Additionally, "will" should be "would" in reported speech, and "for the next morning" is less precise than "by the next morning."

Option c: He asked the mechanic if he will have the car ready by the previous morning. "Will" should be "would" in reported speech, and "previous morning" is incorrect, as "tomorrow morning" should become "the next morning" in the context of reported speech.

Option d: He said the mechanic whether he would has the car ready by the following morning. "Said" is incorrect for a question (should be "asked"), "would has" is grammatically incorrect (should be "would have"), and the structure is awkward.

Hence, the correct answer is option (a).

questions.solution:
The sentence in the Indirect Speech is in Past Perfect Tense.

There are three cases when the Indirect Speech is in Past Perfect Tense.

Tense remains same

Past perfect changes to Present Perfect

Past perfect changes to Simple Past

Case 1: Past Perfect (Subject + had + V3 + Object) tense will be kept intact.

For example:

He said that he had just finished the movie. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "I had just finished the movie" (Direct Speech)

Case 2: Past Perfect (Subject + had + V3 +Object) will be converted into Present Perfect (Subject + has/have + V3 +Object).

For example:

He said that he had got a new job. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "I have got a new job." (Direct Speech)

Case 3: Past Perfect (Subject + had + V3 + Object) will be converted into Past Simple (Subject + V2 + Object).

For example:

He said that Arya had sent him a book. (Indirect Speech)

He said, "Arya sent me a book" (Direct Speech)

The following things in the sentence will change when changed from Indirect Speech to Direct Speech:

· Inverted commas are added, and 'that' is removed.

The reporting verb 'said' will remain as such in the direct form. Options (a), (b) and (c) are incorrect according to the change in tense. The first case is applicable here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Shravan said, "The prisoner had slept throughout the journey."

Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.
